title: The Computer Dance
text:
In 1966, during welcome week at the University of Minnesota, Elaine Walster and her colleagues sold tickets to a dance for incoming students. Buyers were told that a computer would match them with a suitable partner based on questionnaires they filled out about their personality, interests and background. In fact, apart from making sure the man was taller than the woman, the pairs were matched at random.

When each student came to buy a ticket, several researchers quickly and secretly rated their physical attractiveness. The students also took tests of intelligence and personality, and their school records were available. More than seven hundred students came to the dance. During the intermission, they filled out a short questionnaire about their date, and months later the researchers checked whether the couples had gone out again.

The results were blunt. The single best predictor of how much a person liked their date, and wanted to see them again, was simply how attractive the date was. Intelligence, personality measures and social skills predicted almost nothing. Contrary to the researchers' expectation, people did not prefer partners closer to their own level of attractiveness. On a first meeting, at least, looks dominated.
lesson: First impressions are heavily shaped by appearance, more than most of us admit. Give people time beyond the first meeting, since deeper qualities show only later.
people: Elaine Walster, Vera Aronson, Darcy Abrahams, Leon Rottman
source: Walster, E., Aronson, V., Abrahams, D., and Rottman, L. (1966). Importance of physical attractiveness in dating behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(5), 508-516.
